item.title: Mandala-Manifested Meadow of Majestic, Melancholic Madness: Re: Mandala-Manifested Meadow of Majestic, Melancholic Madness
item.content:encoded:
+ Crit lives within
– hide block

Coherence:

Assuming you meant thematic coherence (due to the Understandability section), this article is a bit all over the place. The nuns, the worms, the mass hysteria, etc., none of it feels like it's properly fit together. Moreover, the Mandala's usage feels largely superficial, especially considering that it felt like a Hindu concept was being forced into a largely Christian framework.

Consistency

Everything from the tulpa onward feels as if it's missing context. The stakes necessary for it to work simply aren't there for much of the piece, and it leads to what feels like a slog through events that don't carry any emotional weight.

Dialogue

Dialogue was alright. Only thing of note was that I found it odd:

Operator: Indeed. The phone says that this fluid's effects include but are not limited to:
1.) Loss of inhibitions.
2.) Steady increase in psychosis-type symptoms.
3.) Dizziness.

Having a character suddenly speak in list form feels off.

Clinical tone

It was fine.

Pacing

The pacing is incredibly off. By the IV portion, the piece read like it was near the end, despite being only 1/3rd the way through. It made the chase scene a major slog. Then the dream ends, and it cuts to the second offset, which feels almost entirely disconnected from the events I read in the log. It's for this reason among others that I recommend removing the second offset.

Additionally, how the "FOOTAGE LOST"s break up sections is very disorientating. It leaves a lot of the earlier sections feeling cut off from one another, without a sense of continuity.

Plot

It didn't seem very good.

As noted above, the piece fails to establish the emotional stakes. I don't know who Hero is; I don't know who the tulpa is. Because I as the reader have no real understanding of these characters, I'm not able to care about everything happening to them. The end result is that the plot feels like a slog through a list of things occurring to characters I neither know or care for.

Additionally, none of the plot feels like it's thematically connected to the anomaly at hand. This is a piece about someone attempting to rescue their tulpa from the dreamscape for a good chunk; however, the overarching "eldritch sponge" aspect barely comes up, and it's only really explored in what amounts to a (figurative) footnote in the final offset. This is especially bad as I heavily recommend you remove it for pacing, among other things.

Understandability

I could understand what was happening perfectly fine, up until the final offset. I don't have any advice on how to fix said offset's understandability, as again, I heavily recommend you remove it.

Is the second list-page even necessary, or can I just remove it and shove the plot reveal into the main page via a collapsible?

100% remove it. It feels overly expository, and the note at the end is unnecessary.

Overall

This piece needs extensive restructuring if it wants to work. The thematics don't feel consistent, the piece feels like it's ending a third of the way through, and the characters don't make enough of an impression to justify the plot of the log.

item.title: SCP Draft - A Sleep Paralysis Demon: Re: SCP Draft - A Sleep Paralysis Demon
item.content:encoded:
Overall, the idea feels a bit uninspired. Simply making a sleep paralysis demon an SCP can definitely work, but it could use a bit more originality or a spin of some kind.

+ Some Critique
- Begone

If you are looking to add to the atmosphere or imagery in your article, one really easy way to do this is to have an interview with an individual who experienced the SCP. After the description, include an interview with a civilian or a member of Foundation staff that was affected. (Perhaps this individual had a unique experience with the SCP, thus causing an interview to become necessary) This way you can more easily put the reader in a first person perspective and allow them to experience the horror and imagery you are going for. This doesn't have to be particularly lengthy either.

UPDATE: Following recent discoveries of biological evidence at SCP-XXXX manifestation points, SCP-XXXX is to be re-classified as Explained (See Case Report - XXXX for further details).

Further investigations are to be left solely to the Chicago Police Department.

I'm not sure what you're going for here, although it could just be me. What kind of biological evidence was found at the manifestation points, and why does it warrant a reclassification and handing the investigation over to the police? In my mind, this implies that the SCP is actually a human or group that's doing these bizarre things for some unknown reason. If this is simply meant to be some kind of cliffhanger/ mystery that's left up to the reader's imagination, then it could be made a bit more clear through wording. If this is indeed suppose to imply that there's a human group or individual doing these things, then it would probably be directly stated in the addenda and description.

item.title: Draft: Frozen Corpse and Nervous System: Re: Draft: Frozen Corpse and Nervous System
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for answers to your questions
– hide block

It sounds like I should be focusing less on the open-mystery aspect that lots of SCPs (especially earlier ones) tend to use, and focus more on disclosing a full story with only small amounts of vague subtleties, is that somewhat accurate? Admittedly I am taking inspiration more from Series 1 than the more recent series.

Open mystery is like…fine when you have a concept that supports this: like, SCP-4391 is a relatively recent example of something that's just, openly highly mysterious about what's going on. The problem here is that the mystery of this…just isn't necessarily very interesting? Which is why a more concrete narrative arc is a good idea (which doesn't mean 'don't be subtle', it just means, 'the subtlety has to actually add something')

I'm thinking one of the best ways to clarify the story in the addenda is to turn Addendum 3 into full interviews with the father and the doctor, which will also disclose more origin story material for the skip, and make it more relatable/sympathetic. Does this sound like something that would work? Would the Foundation do something like that, i.e. visit them in person under the guise of a separate government organization, instead of just making a phone call?

My, concern with this is that it feels like it would add a lot of backstory to this without really adding much that's interesting (i.e., that this feels too much like an info dump of material that doesn't necessarily add a tonne).

I can definitely shorten the description by at least 20-25%, maybe almost half. I get the impression that I should instead put almost all of my focus into the addenda. I think 3000 words total would be the high end I should go for, but would that seem disproportionate to put so much of the material into these sections? Most SCPs I see tend not to have more than 5 addenda, unless it's intended as a lengthy epic.

I don't think this is a huge concern tbh. Like, use as many addendum and as many words as you need to convey what you need to: the problem with the description is that it provides a lot of detail that covers how it works exactly that like, the first addendum directly shows in a more effective/interesting manner.

The "closure" I intend to make is that the creature's desire is to achieve closure with the father character by meeting him. This is something that I think the Foundation would never allow even if they understood that's what it wants, which is why I don't end with a solid conclusion, but rather with the indefinite freezing, to imply it never gets what it wants (though I intend to modify the specifics here). Do you disagree, and feel the creature should achieve this?

See, the indefinite freezing can grant closure, it just doesn't here. For it to work, it has to provoke an emotional reaction in the reader: we have to want the SCP to reach the father because we think e.g. it would achieve something, perhaps a sense of closure for the SCP, perhaps a partial/full reversal of the situation, perhaps allowing the SCP to get revenge say; and then for us to be invested in this happening; so that a final note saying e.g. 'due to budget concerns, further testing has been suspended indefinitely.' lands because we actually care.

In the current version, the indefinite freezing doesn't land because it's effectively the status quo already: it's not a new development.

item.title: Draft: Frozen Corpse and Nervous System: Re: Draft: Frozen Corpse and Nervous System
item.content:encoded:
+ show block
– hide block
  • Conprocs: I think you should cut the specific dimensions of the containment unit. Such specific dimensions are always a bad idea… what if it is 6cm smaller than the requirement? Does containment fail then? Instead suggest just saying it is contained in a cryogenic preservation tank and leaving out the dimensions.
    • Moreover, I think you should cut all the bits that are crossed out. I personally think crossing out in a digital document (which this clearly is) makes no sense. This is a living document, so if there was an update, and it is necessary to tell the reader about, break it out into a collapsible. BUT, personally, I would suggest cutting them entirely. As I don’t think you would lose anything.
    • Finally, I would suggest simplifying the closing sentence. Most of those details can be assumed (locking of doors and only approved personnel should be allowed to observe, etc)
  • Redactions: I think you should get rid of all the redactions here. They serve little purpose, just make up or find real world locations… make up dates. Think about it like this, you are reading a classified document and assumedly from a position of approval, so why would the documents be redacted for the reader? Redactions usually only occur when a classified document is released to the public… that’s not what is happening in 99% of SCPs.
  • Description: You’ve got a lot of bloat here, I would suggest trimming it down to roughly 50-60% of the words you currently have. Consider that anything provided just for context is easily cut… the Description should just be what is necessary for the understanding of the story. For example, most of the second paragraph concerning the discovery seems like information we could assume.
    • Also, you want to start off with the primary description… so anything about the discovery should come later.
    • I don’t understand why -1 is designated at all, as there seems to be nothing anomalous about the top half of the corpse.
    • I think there’s way too much information about the lower half’s locomotion.
    • The second to last paragraph seems like speculation, which doesn’t really belong in a description (as this is “what we know” not what “we are wondering about”) and also don’t think it adds much
    • Why does -3 match the genetics of -1 but not -2, isn’t -1 and -2 just two halves of the corpse of a woman?
  • Addendum-A: I think you should format the transcript, to show it as a separate document. There are simplistic templates on the Wiki syntax page: http://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/wiki-syntax#toc5
    • Why would the doctor let it out into the halls? What research purpose would this serve?
  • Addendum-B: I would suggest cutting this entirely, and adding a tiny bit to the transcrpipt like: “vocalization other than Dr. Bosco can be heard. Dr. Bosco does not respond or acknowledge the vocalization.” This would be much creepier, and would suggest people listen to the recording itself. The reason I am suggesting you cut this addendum is its redundant, and suffers from “telling not showing,” especially when you’ve already done the business with the recording.
  • Addendum-C: You don’t really have an ending here, there’s no climax or resolution to the story. A lot of buildup, leading to the revelation that the thing can talk on the audio recording and is searching for its dad… but then you go back and spend three paragraphs trying to figure out who the woman was. Why is it needed to be assumed, is there no fingerprinting, or dental records of this individual? Moreover… I don’t think it’s a satisfying ending to merely try to identify the corpse. We could never know anything about her and it wouldn’t make the article worse…
    • I think you need a stinger of some sort, and some thought needs to be put into how you want this ending to sit with the reader. Is this a haunting piece? Do you want to imply an emotional resolution is possible? As it is, it lands very flat.

item.title: Life Is But A Dream: Update - Unfounded Cannon/SCP-001 proposal
item.content:encoded:
http://scp-sandbox-3.wikidot.com/penton (Life Is But A Dream)

This article is set in the Unfounded Cannon.

My main question is, how would this work as a short SCP-001 proposal set in the Unfounded Cannon? The main idea being that the only SCP in such a reality is one existing in the dreams of Dr. Wondertainment, who ultimately misses the Foundation even though they've never known it in this reality.
